chapter.description: The standard pattern for app-wide state without a library.

blocks.text: Context delivers a value; it does not manage one. Pairing it with `useReducer` gives you a small, predictable store with no dependencies.
Splitting state and dispatch into two contexts is deliberate. `dispatch` never changes identity, so components that only dispatch actions never re-render when the cart changes.

items: Try composition before context; it keeps data flow visible.
Create, provide, consume - and wrap consumption in a custom hook that validates the provider exists.
Memoise object values, or every consumer re-renders on every provider render.
Split state and dispatch, or fast-changing and slow-changing values, into separate contexts.

blocks.text: The next tutorial covers `useReducer` itself in detail, including how to design actions and when a reducer beats a pile of `useState` calls.

previous.title: Context and Re-renders
previous.description: The one performance trap everyone hits, and how to avoid it.

blocks.text: Every component that reads a context re-renders when the provider's `value` changes - and React compares that value by reference.

blocks.caption: Every render of App re-renders every consumer, even if user never changed.

blocks.text: The fix is to memoise the object so its identity is stable while its contents are.
`setUser` is guaranteed stable by React, so it does not need to be in the dependency array - though including it is harmless.
Split contexts that change at different rates
If one part of the value changes constantly and another rarely, put them in separate contexts. Components that only need the stable half stop re-rendering.

blocks.code:
// Changes on every keystroke
<SearchQueryContext.Provider value={query}>
  {/* Changes almost never */}
  <SearchActionsContext.Provider value={actions}>
    <Results />
  </SearchActionsContext.Provider>
</SearchQueryContext.Provider>

blocks.text: Keep the provider high and the tree below it stable
Children passed to a provider as `children` are created by the parent, so they do not re-render just because the provider's value changed - only the consumers do.

If context re-renders are still a real measured problem, that is the point at which a library such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit earns its keep. They let components subscribe to a slice of state instead of the whole value.

blocks.title: Memoise a context value by hand
blocks.instructions: Complete makeValueCache so it returns the same object while the user id is unchanged, and a new object when it changes.

tests.name: The same id returns the same object
tests.code: var g = makeValueCache(); return g({ id: 1 }) === g({ id: 1 });

tests.name: A new id returns a new object
tests.code: var g = makeValueCache(); var a = g({ id: 1 }); return g({ id: 2 }) !== a;

tests.name: The value wraps the user
tests.code: var g = makeValueCache(); var u = { id: 3 }; return g(u).user === u;
